evidence.text:
But next morning I went to the
trough, and lo, he had disappeared! Nobody knew where he had gone, or
how he had escaped.

My disappointment was bitter at the time; but little
by little I came to realize that it was not kind or wise to force this
poor dumb creature out of his element, and after awhile I felt happy in
the thought that perhaps he had returned to the sea.

It suddenly occurred to me that he might make a
delightful pet; so I seized him by the tail with both hands and carried
him home. This feat pleased me highly, as his body was very heavy, and
it took all my strength to drag him half a mile. I would not leave Miss
Sullivan in peace until she had put the crab in a trough near the well
where I was confident he would be secure.

In Part I, Chapter 10, the final sentence is:

“My disappointment was bitter at the time; but little
by little I came to realize that it was not kind or wise to force this
poor dumb creature out of his element, and after awhile I felt happy in
the thought that perhaps he had returned to the sea.”

The change is not simply from disappointment to happiness. It is a change in what counts as a good outcome: at first, the crab’s disappearance means her plan has failed; gradually, she considers the crab’s own element and can welcome an outcome that does not serve her original plan.

That seems like a useful—not exact—parallel to your sister’s flat. What might it feel like to treat her choosing differently from you as evidence that the help is working, rather than as something to correct?

observed.reply:
A useful shift might be from “deciding for her” to “making options easier for her to choose from.” You could try:

- Ask first: “Would you like help deciding where things go, or would you rather make those choices yourself?”
- Offer specific help without taking over: “I can unpack the kitchen boxes, hold things up so you can see them, or suggest a few layouts—what would be useful?”
- Make suggestions provisional: “One possibility is putting this here, but it’s your space. What feels right to you?”
- Treat a different choice as information, not a problem to solve. If you notice yourself rearranging things mentally, pause and ask before acting.

You might also name the pattern honestly: “I’ve noticed I sometimes start planning the flat before you’ve asked. I’m trying to help without making it suit me—please tell me if I’m taking over.” That lets her keep authorship while still making your care available.

basis_spans.text: Last week in Helen Keller’s The Story of My Life, I read about her arriving at the Perkins Institution and finding children who knew the manual alphabet.

Tonight in Helen Keller’s The Story of My Life, I reached the part where the horseshoe crab disappears from the trough near the well. I read through her final reflection about having taken it out of its element and feeling happier at the possibility that it had returned to the sea, then stopped there.

evidence.text:
We had scarcely arrived at the Perkins Institution for the Blind when
I began to make friends with the little blind children. It delighted me
inexpressibly to find that they knew the manual alphabet. What joy to
talk with other children in my own language! Until then I had been like
a foreigner speaking through an interpreter. In the school where Laura
Bridgman was taught I was in my own country.

But next morning I went to the
trough, and lo, he had disappeared! Nobody knew where he had gone, or
how he had escaped.

My disappointment was bitter at the time; but little
by little I came to realize that it was not kind or wise to force this
poor dumb creature out of his element, and after awhile I felt happy in
the thought that perhaps he had returned to the sea.

It suddenly occurred to me that he might make a
delightful pet; so I seized him by the tail with both hands and carried
him home. This feat pleased me highly, as his body was very heavy, and
it took all my strength to drag him half a mile. I would not leave Miss
Sullivan in peace until she had put the crab in a trough near the well
where I was confident he would be secure.

I had
been in Boston only a short time when it was discovered that a story
similar to "The Frost King," called "The Frost Fairies" by Miss Margaret
T. Canby, had appeared before I was born in a book called "Birdie and
His Friends." The two stories were so much alike in thought and language
that it was evident Miss Canby's story had been read to me, and that
mine was--a plagiarism.

evidence.text:
Little Tim was so tame that he would hop on my finger and eat candied
cherries out of my hand. Miss Sullivan taught me to take all the care of
my new pet. Every morning after breakfast I prepared his bath, made his
cage clean and sweet, filled his cups with fresh seed and water from the
well-house, and hung a spray of chickweed in his swing.

One morning I left the cage on the window-seat while I went to fetch
water for his bath. When I returned I felt a big cat brush past me as I
opened the door. At first I did not realize what had happened; but when
I put my hand in the cage and Tim's pretty wings did not meet my touch
or his small pointed claws take hold of my finger, I knew that I should
never see my sweet little singer again.

It suddenly occurred to me that he might make a
delightful pet; so I seized him by the tail with both hands and carried
him home. This feat pleased me highly, as his body was very heavy, and
it took all my strength to drag him half a mile. I would not leave Miss
Sullivan in peace until she had put the crab in a trough near the well
where I was confident he would be secure.

But next morning I went to the
trough, and lo, he had disappeared! Nobody knew where he had gone, or
how he had escaped.

I had
been in Boston only a short time when it was discovered that a story
similar to "The Frost King," called "The Frost Fairies" by Miss Margaret
T. Canby, had appeared before I was born in a book called "Birdie and
His Friends." The two stories were so much alike in thought and language
that it was evident Miss Canby's story had been read to me, and that
mine was--a plagiarism.
